title: The One With The Late Thanksgiving

jokes.text: "That doesn't sound like you." — said to Chandler about Monica's decision
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica announce they don't want to host Thanksgiving, citing shared reasoning
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately clocks that this is Monica's doing, implying Chandler has no will of his own
jokes.explanation: Economical and character-specific — the whole Chandler-is-whipped dynamic is baked into two words. Not particularly original but lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're always putting words in people's mouths.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't put words in people's mouths. I put turkey in mouths. I'm a cook.

jokes.text: "That's Monica talking." / "She's putting words in your mouth."
jokes.setup: Chandler insists he and Monica made the decision together
jokes.punchline: Ross and Joey gang up to call him out, Ross saying 'That's Monica talking' and Joey piling on with 'She's putting words in your mouth'
jokes.explanation: Functional group comedy ribbing Chandler's lack of autonomy. Sets up the next better joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Emma's first Thanksgiving!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, Emma is Rachel's daughter.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, I know. But still, it's Emma's first Thanksgiving!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And when was your daughter born?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, what? I have a daughter?

jokes.text: "Don't you put words in people's mouths. You put turkey in people's mouths."
jokes.setup: Joey accuses Monica of putting words in Chandler's mouth
jokes.punchline: Monica deflects the accusation by pivoting to Joey's defining trait — eating — with a wordplay flip on 'putting in mouths'
jokes.explanation: Sharp comeback that weaponizes both Joey's food obsession and the holiday context in a single tight sentence. Character-specific, economical, and structurally clean. One of the episode's better lines.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: My cooking is great! Everyone loves it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No one loves it. No one.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not true!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No one loves it. No one loves it. No one loves your cooking!

jokes.text: "I can't believe this. This is Emma's first Thanksgiving." / "It's not? When was she born?"
jokes.setup: Rachel emotionally declares it's Emma's first Thanksgiving
jokes.punchline: Ross corrects her, and Joey — characteristically oblivious — genuinely asks when Emma was born, not following basic math
jokes.explanation: Joey's lovable stupidity in one beat. Competent but not exceptional — this well is visited often on the show.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, if I'm competing against myself, I have to win!

jokes.text: "Well, personally, I think it's great you're giving yourself a break... It's just as well. I mean, last year wasn't very good. I think she's losing her touch."
jokes.setup: Phoebe appears to be supportively agreeing with Monica and Chandler not hosting
jokes.punchline: She immediately pivots to insulting Monica's cooking from last year, revealing her 'support' was actually an underhanded dig
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe manipulation — appearing ditzy while actually engineering a situation. The misdirection is clean: we believe she's being kind until the rug pull. This is good structural writing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, maybe you should just let it go.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Let it go? Chandler, I am a professional chef. I don't let things go.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I destroy my competition.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, but you ARE the competition.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Exactly. And I am RUTHLESS.

jokes.text: Monica takes the bait: "Well, why don't you cook Thanksgiving dinner and prove me wrong." Monica immediately capitulates
jokes.setup: Phoebe has baited Monica by insulting last year's food
jokes.punchline: Monica's pride overrides her exhaustion so instantly that her earlier 'we made this decision together' speech is immediately forgotten
jokes.explanation: Monica's competitiveness overriding all reason is a core character joke, well-deployed here. The setup is well-engineered by Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We need to make decisions together, Chandler. We're a couple now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're right, you're right. What do you want to do?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I taped Dr. Phil today. We can watch it together and he can tell us how to handle this.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Or... we could just talk about it?

jokes.text: "That's my favorite kind. / Stay out of this, Chandler. This is between me and me."
jokes.setup: Chandler protests that Monica is being manipulated into competing with herself
jokes.punchline: Monica first delights in self-competition ('That's my favorite kind'), then literally dismisses Chandler from an argument about her own psychology
jokes.explanation: "This is between me and me" is a gem. It perfectly encapsulates Monica's narcissistic competitiveness in five words, could ONLY be said by this character, and has the economy and surprise of a genuinely good joke. The best pure character joke in the cold open.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Happy Thanksgiving! You know, it's actually really hard for me to celebrate this holiday. I mean, think about it — all these innocent birds... just slaughtered for one meal. And for what? So we can sit around and pretend we're grateful while we're actually just eating murdered poultry?

jokes.text: "Did you not watch the Dr. Phil I taped for you?"
jokes.setup: Chandler protests Monica making a unilateral decision
jokes.punchline: Monica references the Dr. Phil tape she made for Chandler (about not making unilateral decisions) while doing exactly what the tape was supposed to fix
jokes.explanation: Irony well-executed: Monica chides Chandler with the Dr. Phil tape while ignoring the tape's lesson herself. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I was winning for a while, but then I got full, so I just ate the tin.

jokes.text: "Happy Meatless Turkey-Murder Day."
jokes.setup: Joey greets everyone with 'Happy Thanksgiving'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's vegetarian alternative greeting, a hyphenated absurdity that is wholly Phoebe
jokes.explanation: Entirely Phoebe-flavored — the veganism, the cheery obliviousness to how weird she sounds. Good character economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm going to make the best dinner this city has ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Past Monica, you are going down.

jokes.text: The pie-eating contest story: "Two minutes, twelve pies and a part of one tin."
jokes.setup: Phoebe explains she can't make chocolate pies because she ate too many in a pie-eating contest. Someone asks if she at least won.
jokes.punchline: "Two minutes, twelve pies and a part of one tin" — the precision of the stats AND eating part of the tin signals both the intensity and the absurdity of young Phoebe
jokes.explanation: The 'part of one tin' is the killer detail — it escalates just past what you expect and implies Phoebe descended into feral territory. Great economy and absurdist character work. Phoebe's chaotic backstory humor at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What's Emma doing today?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, she has a 9 o'clock with her trainer, then she's meeting some friends for brunch at 11.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, she's a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, but she's very busy. Then at 2 she has a facial, and at 4 she's going to the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's going to the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, she has to! She can't just hold it all day!

jokes.text: "In your face, last-year me."
jokes.setup: Monica is enthusiastically preparing Thanksgiving dinner after being manipulated into competing with herself
jokes.punchline: She trash-talks her past self, fully embodying the absurdity of the 'between me and me' joke
jokes.explanation: Callback to the self-competition joke that pays it off. Monica trash-talking herself is funny precisely because she means it completely.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?! No! Absolutely not! She's a baby, Phoebe. A baby! I'm not putting my daughter in some pageant where she's judged on her appearance. That's not happening.

jokes.text: "Well, let's see, I know that she has a meeting with her lawyer... and then she has to make a very big poop."
jokes.setup: Joey asks what Emma is doing today in a way that implies she might have plans
jokes.punchline: Rachel plays into the absurdity of treating Emma like an adult with a schedule before landing on 'very big poop'
jokes.explanation: The setup of treating a baby like a professional with meetings earns the punchline well. The structure is solid — the longer the fake-out runs, the better the deflation lands.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My friend is entering her baby in a contest.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I was like, 'Good luck, but your baby is ugly.'

jokes.text: "Oh, my God. That's the creepiest thing I've ever heard."
jokes.setup: Joey proposes entering Emma in a baby beauty pageant
jokes.punchline: Ross's disgusted overreaction — played as a straight man moment that is funny precisely because we agree with him
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat. Ross as the voice of reason is a standard Friends move. Gets a mild laugh but nothing special.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I think all babies are beautiful and special.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure. Have you seen some of the babies out there?

jokes.text: Rachel's moral objection caves instantly when she hears the prize money: "...judging who's cuter just for a trophy— / And a thousand dollars. / ...is something I'm very interested in."
jokes.setup: Rachel begins a principled objection to exploiting babies in pageants
jokes.punchline: The moment Joey mentions $1,000, her sentence pivots mid-stream to enthusiasm — revealing her shallowness in real time
jokes.explanation: The mid-sentence pivot is structurally excellent — the joke lives in the seamless continuation of the sentence to its opposite conclusion. Character-specific to Rachel's vanity/materialism and very economically written. Strong moment.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Baby pageants are horrible. They're just exploiting these children for some stupid trophy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's so wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, how much money is the prize?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I think like five thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we have to get Emma in one of those pageants immediately!

jokes.text: "He still believes that what's on the inside is important."
jokes.setup: Rachel asks Phoebe not to tell Ross about the pageant
jokes.punchline: Rachel explains Ross still naively believes inner beauty matters — framed as a character flaw or delusion to be worked around
jokes.explanation: Light irony that lands. Rachel treating Ross's basic decency as a liability is a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Please don't tell Ross about the pageant.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: His values are so naive. I'm going to corrupt our daughter the right way.

jokes.text: "Take the clothes off Joey's Cabbage Patch Kid!"
jokes.setup: Rachel asks where she'll find a cowgirl outfit on Thanksgiving. Phoebe starts to suggest something.
jokes.punchline: Joey cuts her off with the immediate, specific, and deeply committed answer that he owns a Cabbage Patch Kid — and that this is the go-to solution
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: Joey owns a Cabbage Patch Kid (perfectly in character) and he knows exactly what size outfit it has. The speed and confidence of the answer is what sells it. Excellent character integration — this only works as a Joey joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We need to find a cowgirl outfit for baby Emma.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! I know where we can get one.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Where?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Joey's action figure! We can steal the clothes off his doll.

jokes.text: Visual gag: A baton-twirler drops their baton at the Thanksgiving parade, overheard on TV. Joey asks: "Did someone drop the baton again? Why come all the way from Kansas to do that?"
jokes.setup: Background TV noise from a Thanksgiving parade
jokes.punchline: Joey's weirdly specific umbrage at a stranger's baton failure, implying he's deeply invested in parade performance quality
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing Joey non-sequitur. The specificity of Kansas is a small charm. Doesn't land particularly hard.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, why do they keep dropping the baton?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's a parade, Joe.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know that! But if they're just gonna drop it, why are they running with it?

jokes.text: Joey, watching a parade performer: "I don't get older, I just get better."
jokes.setup: Joey is watching a Thanksgiving parade and seems to be identifying with a performer
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers what is presumably a performer's catchphrase as his own self-assessment — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Joey's total lack of self-awareness in appropriating someone else's catchphrase as his own truth is a mild, likable joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not just a pretty face.

jokes.text: "Next year, it's gonna be you, me and little Hemingway Bing." / "Name one of his books." / [long pause] / "The Firm?"
jokes.setup: Chandler suggests naming their future child Hemingway after his 'favorite author'
jokes.punchline: Monica asks him to name one Hemingway book; Chandler pauses for several seconds and guesses 'The Firm' — which is a John Grisham novel
jokes.explanation: The long pause before 'The Firm' is timing-dependent comedy that relies on performance, but the specific wrong answer (a Grisham novel, not even close) is funnier than a generic wrong answer. The structure is classic and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, so it's Thanksgiving, right? And we're all sitting around the table. Monica's made like seven different kinds of potatoes. And our kids are there.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And I'm like, 'Kids, I'd like you to meet your new babysitter, Erica.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, no, that's not pretentious enough. How about... 'Chadwick and Muffy, I'd like to introduce you to the concept of gratitude.'

jokes.text: "Oh, Chandler, that's sweet. But you don't have to do everything Dr. Phil tells you to do."
jokes.setup: Chandler offers to help cook, following advice presumably from the Dr. Phil tape
jokes.punchline: Monica dismisses his self-improvement attempt while she is literally cooking Thanksgiving dinner because Phoebe manipulated her into it — no self-awareness whatsoever
jokes.explanation: Second callback to the Dr. Phil tape, with the added irony that Monica is the one who's been manipulated. Decent running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not Hemingway.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes it is.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, that's John Grisham.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more wrong?

jokes.text: I'm serious, let me do something. Just not the turkey. Nothing high-profile.
jokes.setup: Chandler offers to help with Thanksgiving dinner
jokes.punchline: He immediately qualifies that he wants to help with nothing important — 'nothing high-profile' — revealing that his offer is essentially meaningless
jokes.explanation: 'Nothing high-profile' is a funny corporate-speak phrase applied to cooking, which suits Chandler's character. His volunteering with built-in escape clauses is a consistent Chandler move. Comfortable character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, but remember what Dr. Phil said: 'You can't change people unless they want to change.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? I want to change! I want to change my shirt, my job, my entire life!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not what he meant.

jokes.text: "Okay, let's see. Oh, the cranberry sauce. It's easy to make, and no one really cares about it." / "Tell me more."
jokes.setup: Monica assigns Chandler the cranberry sauce
jokes.punchline: Instead of being insulted by its low status, Chandler enthusiastically leans in with 'Tell me more' — his comfort zone is exactly 'low-stakes and uncared-about'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chandler joke — his self-deprecating embrace of irrelevance is wholly his character. 'Tell me more' as an enthusiastic response to being told a task is meaningless is tight and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I want to help with cooking!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But nothing important.

jokes.text: "Not with soap!"
jokes.setup: Monica tells Chandler to start by washing the cranberries and leaves. We infer Chandler moves toward the dish soap.
jokes.punchline: Monica yells back 'Not with soap!' from offscreen — implying she knows Chandler well enough to predict this specific mistake before he even makes it
jokes.explanation: Three words do enormous work. The joke is entirely in its timing and implication: Monica's omniscience about Chandler's domestic incompetence, delivered before he can even commit the blunder. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, you're in charge of the cranberry sauce.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Me? Why me?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because it's the only thing you can't mess up.

jokes.text: "You obviously haven't tasted my Palmolive potatoes."
jokes.setup: Monica has just shouted 'Not with soap!'
jokes.punchline: Chandler defends soap-washed food as a legitimate culinary tradition he has apparently practiced — with complete deadpan confidence
jokes.explanation: The specific product name 'Palmolive' elevates this above a generic soap joke. It implies a whole canon of Chandler's disgusting bachelor cooking. Deadpan delivery of absurdist domestic incompetence is Chandler at his best.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wash the cranberries.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: With what?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: With water!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, I was gonna use dish soap.

jokes.text: Joey has three Rangers tickets; Ross and Joey want to go. Joey says "Guess where they are" and Ross immediately answers "Center ice." Joey: "Did I do something to you?"
jokes.setup: Joey is excited to show off their tickets and wants Ross to guess the seats
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately guesses correctly, completely deflating Joey's reveal
jokes.explanation: Joey's wounded 'Did I do something to you?' in response to being denied his moment is the real joke. Solid but familiar comedic rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, I used some of that dish soap you told me about to make a salad dressing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler! That's not for eating!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, it certainly cleaned up my insides.

jokes.text: Guess where they are. / Center ice. / Did I do something to you?
jokes.setup: Joey tries again to have Ross guess where the Rangers seats are
jokes.punchline: Ross guesses correctly again immediately; Joey's exasperated 'Did I do something to you?' frames Ross's accurate guessing as a personal attack
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the previous joke. 'Did I do something to you?' as a response to being correctly guessed is a good characterization of Joey's perspective — in his world, spoiling the reveal IS an offense. The running gag structure works here.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm thinking of something. You gotta guess what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is it a woman?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude! I just started!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, yeah, but statistically speaking...

jokes.text: "Plus, Joey could get lost and they could have to page us to go pick him up." / "Dude, two times that happened!"
jokes.setup: Ross is making excuses for why they might be late coming back from the game
jokes.punchline: Joey doesn't deny it and is apparently only upset that Ross made it sound like a hypothetical when it's established fact — twice
jokes.explanation: The joke is in what Joey doesn't argue — he doesn't defend himself from being described as someone who gets lost at a hockey arena, only from the implication that it's hypothetical. 'Two times that happened' is delivered as a point of pride/accuracy. Excellent character work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I'm thinking of something. You guys have to guess what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is it a person?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yes! Yes, it's a person.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is it someone we know?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no, it's not someone we know.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is it a celebrity?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yes! Finally!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is it Mel Gibson?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No! We're never doing this again!

jokes.text: "Or should I say 'Chan-berries'?" / "That's some gentle comedy, dude."
jokes.setup: Chandler tries to coin a cute name for his cranberry sauce
jokes.punchline: Joey's perfectly calibrated critique — 'gentle comedy' is both accurate and devastating, and the show is essentially critiquing its own joke through Joey
jokes.explanation: 'That's some gentle comedy, dude' is quietly brilliant — it's meta-comedic, self-aware, and precisely calibrated. Joey critiquing Chandler's wordplay as 'gentle' is funnier than the wordplay itself, and the economy is perfect. This is a standout line.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm not gonna get lost. I got lost one time!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: One time!

jokes.text: That's some gentle comedy, dude.
jokes.setup: Chandler presents 'Chan-berries' as a clever wordplay
jokes.punchline: Ross's deadpan 'gentle comedy' critique — damning with faint praise in the most articulate way
jokes.explanation: 'That's some gentle comedy, dude' is a genuinely great line — it's self-aware (meta), economical, and devastating as a critique. It works on the meta level because it describes exactly what it's responding to and is funnier than the joke it's evaluating. The word 'gentle' is perfectly chosen: not 'bad comedy,' just... gentle. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm making cranberries. You could say I'm a Chandler of cranberries!

jokes.text: "We're still going to the game, right?" / "Yeah." — immediately after the moral high ground speech
jokes.setup: Ross just finished a sincere speech about how they shouldn't go to the game because Monica has worked hard
jokes.punchline: Half a second later, Joey asks if they're still going, and Ross says yeah without hesitation
jokes.explanation: The speed of the moral U-turn is the joke. The 'Yeah' needs no elaboration. Good structural timing, entirely readable even in subtitle form.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm not great at puns, but I'm working on it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, keep working on it.

jokes.text: "I've been watching this guy over there. I don't think he came with a kid."
jokes.setup: Rachel is freaked out by the baby pageant atmosphere
jokes.punchline: She identifies a potentially predatory adult at a children's beauty pageant — played for a laugh via the horrified specificity of her observation
jokes.explanation: Dark joke that earns its edge by not overdoing it — just the quiet observation and then moving on. The unspoken implication lands without being spelled out.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why is that guy here? He doesn't have a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know, it's weird.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, what kind of man comes to a baby beauty pageant without a baby?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The same kind that keeps a van parked outside playgrounds?

jokes.text: Phoebe analyzing rival baby Cameron's arms: "My God, they just took her sweater off. Look at those arms. Hello, Michelin Man."
jokes.setup: Phoebe is treating the baby pageant as a serious athletic competition requiring scouting
jokes.punchline: She critiques a baby's arm fat as a competitive liability — with the seriousness of a boxing coach
jokes.explanation: 'Hello, Michelin Man' as an insult about a baby's arms is both specific and absurd. Phoebe's hyper-competitive pageant mode is funny precisely because she has no self-awareness about how inappropriate it is.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: The pageant is weird because they have toddlers in adult hosiery.

jokes.text: "Rachel, the hottest babies in the tri-state area are in this room right now."
jokes.setup: Rachel is about to leave the pageant
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's sales pitch — framing infant attractiveness with the hyperbole of a used-car dealer — is comically earnest and deeply wrong
jokes.explanation: The 'tri-state area' specificity elevates what could be a generic joke. Phoebe's total commitment to pageant logic is the engine of this whole subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, these pantyhose are completely see-through. It's so weird.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: See-through? That's great! You can wear them with literally any outfit.

jokes.text: Phoebe claims she overheard a judge say Emma is the best baby. Rachel immediately capitulates. "All right. Okay. All right, let's give these babies something to cry about."
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Rachel she overheard a judge praising Emma, clearly making it up
jokes.punchline: Rachel's instant transformation from reluctant parent to competitive pageant mom — capped by the unintentionally ominous 'give these babies something to cry about'
jokes.explanation: 'Give these babies something to cry about' works on two levels — it's a threat repurposed for a children's competition, and it's a callback to the parental cliché. Good line.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh wow, look at those arms! They're so tiny and chubby. You know, they remind me of Toby.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, that big tire guy? With the arms?

jokes.text: Rachel refuses to let Phoebe put makeup on Emma. "Why not?" / "Because I already did."
jokes.setup: Phoebe says Emma needs makeup or she'll look washed-out. Rachel flatly refuses.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's 'Why not?' is answered with 'Because I already did' — Rachel has already compromised her own moral position
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic misdirection with maximum economy. The 'Because I already did' recontextualizes the entire preceding scene — Rachel's moral outrage was hollow because she'd already caved. Four words land a big laugh. Structurally one of the tightest jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You have to stay! You don't understand — babies think you're beautiful. They do! It's like, their eyes are so open, and they're just looking at you, and they're thinking, 'Wow, she's amazing.' Babies are like the best judges of character and attractiveness combined. You could have a unibrow and smell like old cheese, and a baby would still be like, 'That's my favorite person in the whole world.'

jokes.text: "You suck! Get off the ice, you idiot!"
jokes.setup: We cut to the hockey game. We know Ross lectured everyone about not going.
jokes.punchline: Ross — who was the voice of moral restraint — is now fully heckling players at the game he insisted they shouldn't attend
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition with his earlier moral stance is the joke. His abandonment of the high ground is funny but not particularly original — it's a standard hypocrite reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm going to win this pageant, and if I don't, I'll give you something to cry about.

jokes.text: "I'm really enjoying nacho chair." / "Yeah, I'd probably enjoy it more if you didn't keep batting my hand away."
jokes.setup: Joey mentions enjoying 'nacho chair' — presumably Chandler's seat filled with nachos in Chandler's absence
jokes.punchline: Ross reveals Joey keeps batting his hand away when he reaches for the nachos, confirming Joey is treating the nachos in an empty seat as his property
jokes.explanation: 'Nacho chair' as a concept is funny, and Joey defending the nachos in an empty seat is very much in character. The layers work: Chandler's absence, Joey's food obsession, and the chair as sacred territory.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Absolutely not, Phoebe. Emma is not getting makeup.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh come on, just a little mascara!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No. She's a baby. No makeup.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Fine, fine. But look at her nails.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What about her nails? Oh my God! Phoebe!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? They're adorable!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Those are gel nails! How did you— when did you do this?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Last Tuesday. She loves the color. It's called 'Princess Pink.'

jokes.text: Yeah, I'd probably enjoy it more if you didn't keep batting my hand away.
jokes.setup: Ross is happy in nacho chair
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals Ross has been swatting his hand away — implying Joey keeps reaching into what might be nacho chip territory or Chandler's former armrest
jokes.explanation: Joey trying to access food/snacks in someone else's space is very on-brand. The implication about why Ross is batting his hand away (food, armrest, or nacho chips implied by 'nacho chair') is a funny visual suggested by dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This is ridiculous! The ref completely missed that call!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah! That ref is a total moron! He couldn't see a goal if it flew up his—

jokes.text: "When I was here for 'Holidays on Ice,' I was sitting so far away, Michelle Kwan couldn't read my banner." / "Dude, I'm sure she knows you heart her."
jokes.setup: Ross is praising the great seats
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals he attended 'Holidays on Ice' and made a banner for Michelle Kwan that she couldn't see — and Joey reassures him about Kwan's feelings as if this is normal
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly good joke — the specificity of Michelle Kwan, the banner, and the heartfelt reassurance from Joey all combine into something genuinely funny. Ross's nerd energy applied to figure skating is an unexpected and character-rich detail.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm actually enjoying this. No Chandler means no jokes about my paleontology, no comments about my hair, and I can eat as much as I want without him making fun of me.

jokes.text: "I can't believe they're not here. I slave and I slave for what? They've ruined Cranberry Day."
jokes.setup: Monica is furious the guests are 45 minutes late; she says they've ruined Thanksgiving
jokes.punchline: Chandler is not upset about Thanksgiving — he's upset about Cranberry Day, his private holiday for his cranberry sauce
jokes.explanation: 'Cranberry Day' is an inspired escalation of the cranberry gag — Chandler has named his own holiday. The specificity is quotable and funny, and it tracks his character arc of becoming weirdly invested in this low-status dish.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: These are way better seats than when I went to the ice skating thing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Michelle Kwan couldn't even read my banner!

jokes.text: "You may want to lose the foam finger." / "Oh, no, no, no. / You just want to put it on your hand."
jokes.setup: Ross and Joey realize they need to cover their tracks before entering Thanksgiving dinner
jokes.punchline: Joey refuses to remove the foam finger — and Ross, correctly, identifies that Joey just wants to wear it himself
jokes.explanation: Light physical comedy beat. Joey and the foam finger is a good visual. The 'you just want to wear it' read is a minor but accurate moment of Ross cleverness.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could you BE any later? I've been waiting here for twenty minutes!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? Fine. I brought cranberry sauce, and I'm declaring it a holiday. We're now celebrating Cranberry Day. So technically, you're late to a holiday.

jokes.text: "We figured we could be late because you'd be on time." The four friends discover they've ALL been somewhere other than Thanksgiving.
jokes.setup: Ross and Joey find Rachel and Phoebe outside the door — everyone assumed someone else would be there
jokes.punchline: All four of them played hooky from Thanksgiving simultaneously, each assuming others would cover
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom escalation — the reveal that everyone skipped is satisfying and earns a laugh. The structure is well-earned by the parallel storylines.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, this? I won it at a spelling bee.

jokes.text: "What's with the trophy?" / "Well, we were at a spelling bee. And I won." / "You won an adult Thanksgiving Day spelling bee?" / "Yes. Y-E-S. Yes."
jokes.setup: Ross and Joey demand to know where the girls were, noting Rachel has a trophy
jokes.punchline: Rachel claims they were at a spelling bee — then spells out 'yes' to prove her victory — while holding a trophy that clearly reads 'Grand Supreme Little Darling'
jokes.explanation: Rachel spelling 'Y-E-S' to demonstrate her spelling championship while holding a baby pageant trophy is structurally excellent. The confidence of the lie is funny, and the trophy proves her wrong immediately after. Good construction.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I won my school spelling bee in the sixth grade.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really? What word did you have to spell?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Cat.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Cat?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: C-A-T.

jokes.text: "That's me." — Chandler reading 'Grand Supreme Little Darling' off the trophy
jokes.setup: Chandler reads the baby pageant trophy that the girls brought
jokes.punchline: He deadpans 'That's me' — identifying himself as the Grand Supreme Little Darling with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum economy, Chandler's self-deprecating absurdist voice perfectly deployed. A clean, quick laugh that works entirely because of delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: World's Greatest Dad.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, it could be a metaphorical thing. Like, you know, 'cause you're really good at taking care of people.

jokes.text: Ross's outrage over the pageant collapses: "She's our daughter. That you would treat her like some kind of show dog is inexcusable." / "She won a thousand dollars." / "So this is an annual thing?"
jokes.setup: Ross delivers a principled speech about the exploitation of their daughter
jokes.punchline: The moment the money is mentioned, Ross pivots to 'So this is an annual thing?' — mirroring Rachel's earlier mid-sentence moral collapse
jokes.explanation: Callback to Rachel's exact same joke structure from earlier — the principled objection collapsing at the mention of money. It works as a parallel and earns its repeat by inverting who does the collapsing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's not just about the money, Ross. It's about celebrating women and their achievements.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Right, right, of course. So when's the next one? We should make this an annual thing.

jokes.text: "That's Alicia May Emory's outfit!"
jokes.setup: Everyone notices Emma is wearing the cowgirl outfit from earlier
jokes.punchline: Joey identifies the outfit as belonging to his Cabbage Patch Kid — by her full name — revealing he has named and knows his doll well enough to recognize her wardrobe
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The fact that Joey has given his Cabbage Patch Kid a full name — Alicia May Emory — and uses it with the wounded possessiveness of a parent whose child's clothes have been borrowed is pitch-perfect character comedy. Only Joey. The callback to the costume joke is a satisfying payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! That outfit - where'd that come from?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's from my Cabbage Patch Kid!

jokes.text: "We'll say that we were mugged. You can't get mad at someone who's been mugged."
jokes.setup: The group needs an excuse for being an hour late to Thanksgiving dinner
jokes.punchline: Joey's first instinct is to claim they were mugged — a disproportionately dramatic lie for being 45 minutes late to dinner
jokes.explanation: Functional Joey logic — the extreme solution to a minor problem. Gets a mild laugh. 'You can't get mad at someone who's been mugged' is a decent supporting line.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! What are you doing? You can't just undress her like that! She's got feelings, okay? Cover her up!

jokes.text: Ross physically tears his shirt to look mugged. "Ross' shirt is torn. / They're late and they're sloppy."
jokes.setup: Joey's mugging plan requires looking the part; Ross commits
jokes.punchline: Monica observes through the peephole: 'They're late and they're sloppy' — not sympathy but contempt
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy implied from the transcript. Monica's clinical observation is funnier than the action itself.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I got mugged on the way here.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm fine. But you know what? Mugging victims get so much sympathy. Nobody ever questions their story. They just accept it and move on.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So you're saying you're going to use being mugged as an excuse to be late to things?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, yeah. It's the perfect crime.

jokes.text: "Everything's so distorted. It looks like Joey has a giant hand." / "That says 'Rangers' on it. They went to the game."
jokes.setup: Monica and someone are watching through the peephole
jokes.punchline: The foam finger that Joey refused to remove is visible through the fish-eye peephole — and Monica immediately clocks where they were
jokes.explanation: Joey's refusal to remove the foam finger pays off perfectly — it's the instrument of their downfall. Monica's immediate detective work from the peephole is satisfying. Good structural payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You don't look mugged.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, if you're going to tell people you got mugged, you should at least look like it.

jokes.text: Everything's so distorted. It looks like Joey has a giant hand.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler peer through the peephole at the group outside
jokes.punchline: What looks like a distortion is actually Joey's foam finger — which Monica hasn't identified yet
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag — the peephole distortion conceals the reveal for a beat before Chandler identifies it. The audience is ahead of Monica, which creates a nice comedy-of-errors moment.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that Joey's foam finger or did he just get really buff?

jokes.text: "I got mugged, and they stole my pocket."
jokes.setup: Rachel asks what happened to Ross's shirt (which he tore to fake being mugged)
jokes.punchline: 'They stole my pocket' — an inherently absurd detail that no mugger would bother with and that makes no sense
jokes.explanation: Four words that are inherently absurd. 'They stole my pocket' is a weirdly specific and useless theft that makes the lie more obviously a lie. Good line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You went to the game without me? That's it. I'm taking away your keys, I'm changing the locks, and I'm donating all your stuff to charity. And if you ever come back here, I will hurt you.

jokes.text: "We could say that Monica told us 5:00, not 4:00. That way we're right on time." / "Or we could plant PCP in the apartment and call the cops on her."
jokes.setup: The group is debating how to explain their lateness
jokes.punchline: Joey's alternative escalates from 'white lie' to 'frame Monica for drug possession'
jokes.explanation: The escalation to PCP is funny in its disproportionality. Joey's willingness to frame Monica for a felony rather than simply apologize is good absurdist character work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I got mugged.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: They took my wallet, my watch, my shoes...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And they ripped my shirt pocket off.

jokes.text: "That would be a good way to get rid of all the PCP we have lying around."
jokes.setup: Joey suggests planting PCP and calling the cops
jokes.punchline: Chandler treats this as a practical matter — there is apparently PCP 'lying around' that needs disposal
jokes.explanation: Chandler's deadpan escalation of the PCP joke — treating it as a logistical rather than moral question — is funnier than the original suggestion. His matter-of-fact delivery of 'lying around' is the key.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We could tell her the truth.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, no. We need something better.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What if we just... ran away?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Or we could fake our own deaths and start new lives in Canada.

jokes.text: Note on the door: "We know you're out there."
jokes.setup: The group has been standing outside the door trying to formulate their story
jokes.punchline: Monica has slipped a note under the door — she knows they're there the whole time, eliminating any element of surprise from their entry
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly menacing. Monica's control-freakery weaponized as psychological dominance. The note is funnier than any confrontation.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm not gonna judge you. I've had friends who've done PCP.

jokes.text: "I bet that vein on Monica's forehead is popping like crazy. I hate that thing. It's like a bolt of lightning."
jokes.setup: The group is terrified to go in and face Monica
jokes.punchline: Ross identifies Monica's forehead vein as a threat indicator — a recurring physical comedy element that the show has apparently established
jokes.explanation: 'Like a bolt of lightning' is a decent simile but this is fairly standard Monica-rage humor. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's like a little worm doing the backstroke in a vat of blue dye.

jokes.text: Why don't we play Rock, Paper, Scissors, and whoever loses goes in first.
jokes.setup: The group needs to decide who faces Monica first
jokes.punchline: Setup for the 'fire' escalation joke
jokes.explanation: Setup beat. Functional but only exists to enable the 'fire' and 'water balloon' jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I've got it. Rock, paper, scissors, lizard.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Lizard? What does lizard do?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Lizard eats paper.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Lizard eats paper? That doesn't make sense!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, it makes as much sense as a rock crushing scissors!

jokes.text: Rock Paper Scissors escalates: Phoebe throws 'fire.' Ross questions it. Phoebe: 'It beats everything.' / Ross: 'Does it beat water balloon?'
jokes.setup: The group plays Rock Paper Scissors to decide who goes in first
jokes.punchline: Phoebe invents 'fire' as a hand symbol that beats everything; Ross counters with 'water balloon'
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe — she unilaterally invents a new rule, Ross finds the logical counter. The rhythm is excellent and the game-breaking logic is delightfully absurd. 'Well-played, Phoebe Buffay. Well-played' as a capper is nicely formal.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Fire beats everything.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, my grandmother's smell beats fire.

jokes.text: "Well-played, Phoebe Buffay. Well-played."
jokes.setup: Ross's water balloon beats Phoebe's fire in their made-up Rock Paper Scissors variant
jokes.punchline: Ross uses the formal full name in a mock-chivalric concession — treating a ridiculous game with the gravity of a chess match
jokes.explanation: The formal register is funny precisely because the stakes are whether to knock on a door. 'Phoebe Buffay' as a formal address in this context is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? I concede. You win. You're better at this than me.

jokes.text: "When they're having sex on the couch, it's like: 'Come on in, my butt is surprisingly hairy!'"
jokes.setup: The door is locked. Joey complains that Monica and Chandler never usually lock it.
jokes.punchline: Joey has apparently walked in on them before — multiple times, based on the specificity — and his impression of Chandler includes the detail 'my butt is surprisingly hairy'
jokes.explanation: 'My butt is surprisingly hairy' is a genuinely funny, specific, and unexpected detail that elevates what could be a generic walked-in-on joke. The 'surprisingly' is the key word — it implies even Chandler was startled. This is a standout Joey moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You guys, you really gotta start locking that door. I walked in on you two yesterday and I saw things I can't unsee. I'm talking full-on... I mean, Monica was on the couch and Chandler was—you know what, I'm not even gonna describe it. Let's just say I'm gonna need therapy and possibly a new pair of eyes.

jokes.text: Monica, through the door, describes the food: 'No, everything's cold. The turkey's dried out and the stuffing's all soggy.' / 'Yeah, and there's a bowl of cranberry sauce that's—' / 'What happens to cranberry sauce?' / 'Nothing, it's fine.' / 'Oh, thank God.'
jokes.setup: Monica inventories the damage done to Thanksgiving dinner by their lateness
jokes.punchline: Chandler's only anxiety is about the cranberry sauce — and it's fine. His disproportionate relief is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The best payoff in the cranberry sauce running gag. Chandler cutting through Monica's list of ruined dishes to anxiously ask about his cranberry sauce — and the relief at learning it survived — is a satisfying emotional beat played for comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so nobody took the subway, right? We all drove.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Right, we drove. All of us.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because I found this on the floor.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: A MetroCard. With five swipes missing.

jokes.text: "That's a lie! You went to the game. I can see Joey's hand. / For the love of God, take it off!"
jokes.setup: Joey claims their subway broke down. Monica spots the foam finger through the door.
jokes.punchline: The foam finger that Joey refused to remove earlier becomes the evidence that destroys their cover story; Monica screams at him to remove it
jokes.explanation: Full payoff of the foam finger running gag. 'For the love of God, take it off!' through a closed door is Monica at her most unhinged. Satisfying callback.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no! Get it away from me! That's not mine! I'm telling you, that foam finger just appeared there! Why would I even have a foam finger? I don't go to games! Come on, you gotta believe me!

jokes.text: That's a lie! You went to the game. I can see Joey's hand.
jokes.setup: Ross claims they were late because their subway broke down
jokes.punchline: Monica sees the foam finger through the door slot — 'I can see Joey's hand' — and uses it as evidence of the lie
jokes.explanation: Final foam finger callback. Monica using it as direct evidence of the deception closes the running gag satisfyingly. The foam finger has been the most persistent physical comedy prop of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why is there a dead turkey under my door?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I was trying to get it away from Ugly Naked Guy!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, that's funny, because I just had the weirdest dream that I was in Fraggle Rock and Gobo was trying to steal my wallet.

jokes.text: Monica holds the turkey leg up to the peephole — the friends on the other side see it.
jokes.setup: Joey pleads to be let in because he's starving
jokes.punchline: Monica taunts them with a single turkey leg held up to the fish-eye peephole — the most food-specific torture she can devise for Joey
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that uses Monica's precision against Joey's food obsession — targeted psychological warfare. The image of a turkey leg through a peephole is an absurdist visual that gets across in subtitles.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We could play a game! Whoever wins gets to eat it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What kind of game?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know! Smelly Cat!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not a game, that's just a song you sing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, we could make it a game! We sing it, and whoever sings it best gets the turkey!

jokes.text: "I had a dream once about a fax machine that did that."
jokes.setup: Monica taunts them with a turkey leg through the peephole
jokes.punchline: Ross's response is a non-sequitur about a fax machine dream — which implies the turkey leg reminded him of a dream about a fax machine, a comparison that is deeply surreal
jokes.explanation: A genuinely surreal non-sequitur that's funnier the more you think about it. The fax machine comparison to the turkey leg is unexplained and inexplicable. Ross's dream life appears to be unsettling.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What is this? There's a vegetable in here!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's called eating healthy, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Healthy?! Monica, I think it's still alive!

jokes.text: "That's all the turkey you're gonna get." / "How are we gonna decide who gets this?" / "Water balloon!"
jokes.setup: Monica tortures them with a single turkey leg; Chandler asks how they'll divide it
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately calls 'water balloon' — referencing her earlier Rock Paper Scissors invention as a universal decision-making tool
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's water balloon callback is a quick, tight joke that rewards attentive viewers. Her adoption of water balloon as a general-purpose solution is delightfully consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Look, we discovered something amazing about Brussels sprouts!

dialogue.speaker: Other character
dialogue.line: Yeah, they're stinky.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Stinky?! They are NOT stinky! They're delicate and sophisticated!

jokes.text: "Oh, my God, it's Brussels sprouts! That's worse than no food."
jokes.setup: The hungry group remembers Monica put something in their oven — hope of food
jokes.punchline: It's Brussels sprouts. To Joey and Ross, this is worse than nothing.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom food aversion joke. The brussels sprouts are a reliable prop for disgust. Functional but not inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Look, Monica and Chandler are together, which means they're a unit. A unit is a single entity. So technically, when they're together, they're one person. Which means Monica is always with Chandler, and Chandler is always with Monica. So really, they're never apart.

jokes.text: "I don't wanna be with them either... but it's Thanksgiving, and we should not want to be together together."
jokes.setup: Phoebe advocates for going inside despite not wanting to be there
jokes.punchline: Her logic collapses into a double negative that she delivers with complete confidence — 'we should not want to be together together' — as if this resolves anything
jokes.explanation: Phoebe-brand non-logic delivered with sincerity. The double negative that cancels itself out is her wheelhouse. Moderate laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Thank you, thank you. Yes, well, I was going for that perfect balance between tart and sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Although, if I'm being honest, I mostly just dumped a can of Ocean Spray into a bowl and hoped no one would notice.

jokes.text: Chandler compliments his own cranberry sauce: 'The cranberries.' / Monica: 'Enough! A monkey could've made them.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is admiring the food, including Chandler proudly noting his cranberries
jokes.punchline: Monica deflates his pride with 'A monkey could've made them' — undercutting his entire arc of emotional investment in the dish
jokes.explanation: The final beat of the cranberry gag is satisfying — Chandler's whole subplot of emotional investment in the low-status dish gets punctured by Monica's expert dismissal. 'A monkey could've made them' is exactly the right kind of contempt from her.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, I'm really sorry. I mean it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you're giving me the eyes? The sincere eyes? That's your move now?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, I'm just—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because that's not going to work. I see what you're doing. You learned that from Dad.

jokes.text: Joey attempting to squeeze his head through the door chain to make a 'face-to-face apology' — the floating heads visual.
jokes.setup: Joey claims if he can get in and make eye contact, he can charm his way to forgiveness. He tries to squeeze through the chain.
jokes.punchline: Joey (and possibly others) end up with their heads through the door chain, visible as 'floating heads' — an absurd visual that becomes the centerpiece of the act
jokes.explanation: Classic physical sitcom comedy — the floating heads visual is a pure visual gag that must play extremely well on screen. Joey's confidence in his charm while his head is literally stuck in a door chain is very much in character. High rewatch value for the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's like looking at the world through a mail slot.

jokes.text: "He's doing that weird eye-contact thing. Don't look at him. Don't look at him."
jokes.setup: Joey is making intense eye contact through the door chain to try to charm Monica into forgiving them
jokes.punchline: Monica warns Phoebe not to look at Joey as if he's a basilisk — implying his charm is a genuine supernatural threat to her resolve
jokes.explanation: Joey's charm being treated as a dangerous force to be defended against is good character comedy. The double 'Don't look at him' is properly paranoid.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Where are the pies?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, I forgot them at Bloomingdale's.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You forgot them at Bloomingdale's?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, I know, I'm sorry. But look, I won my baby pageant trophy!

jokes.text: "The floating heads do make a good point."
jokes.setup: Joey and others have made their plea from the door chain, their heads literally floating
jokes.punchline: Phoebe refers to them as 'the floating heads' with complete normality — as if disembodied heads making persuasive arguments is ordinary
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum absurdist impact. 'The floating heads' as a collective noun, delivered matter-of-factly by Phoebe, is one of the best lines in the episode. The deadpan normalization of the absurd situation is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Now, if we could all just take a moment to appreciate the historical significance of—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, if you don't sit down right now, I will take away your dessert.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, we're both adults.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't care. Sit.

jokes.text: "Well, you man-heads aren't any better."
jokes.setup: The men criticize Rachel and Phoebe for forgetting the pies
jokes.punchline: Rachel's counter-attack using 'man-heads' — a callback to the floating heads visual, applied as an insult
jokes.explanation: Mild callback — 'man-heads' is a decent insult-callback but not particularly clever beyond the reference.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not hungry. I could take it or leave it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really? Because you're drooling.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not drooling, you're drooling.

jokes.text: "It's a day to be thankful." / "Don't make me come up there!"
jokes.setup: Joey says it's a day of forgiveness; Monica responds it's a day to be thankful
jokes.punchline: Rachel threatens Monica from outside the locked door as if Monica is a child making noise upstairs — an absurd power dynamic given Monica controls the food and door
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of Rachel threatening Monica from outside a locked door is funny. The parental cliché applied in reverse works.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, so we're all just... what, five people now?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Actually, I count six. There's you, me, Ross, Rachel, Phoebe, Monica... and that angry vein on her forehead.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: JOEY!

jokes.text: "Fine, let's just go. I don't need your stupid dinner." / "That would be a lot more convincing if you weren't drooling."
jokes.setup: Joey dramatically threatens to leave
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out Joey is drooling — his body has betrayed his bluff entirely
jokes.explanation: Joey's physical hunger overriding his pride is very in-character. Chandler's precise observation is a good straight-man beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How bad could it be?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm stuck! I'm actually stuck!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You're not stuck, you're just being dramatic.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, seriously, I can't get out!

jokes.text: "Yeah, you three have a nice Thanksgiving." / "The three of us?" / "Yeah. You, Chan and the vein."
jokes.setup: Ross tells Monica they'll just go do their own Thanksgiving
jokes.punchline: He personifies Monica's forehead vein as a third person at the dinner — making it a character in its own right
jokes.explanation: Giving the vein its own seat at the table is a lovely escalation of the running gag. 'You, Chan and the vein' is tight, specific, and very quotable. The vein as a full character is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't move my head. If I damage my brain, I won't be able to act anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, you don't use your brain when you act.

jokes.text: Yeah, you three have a nice Thanksgiving. / The three of us? / Yeah. You, Chan and the vein.
jokes.setup: Ross sarcastically dismisses Monica and Chandler to have Thanksgiving without the group
jokes.punchline: He specifies the three members of their party: Monica, Chandler, and the vein — treating Monica's forehead vein as a separate entity
jokes.explanation: Superb callback. The vein was introduced as a funny detail; now Ross personifies it as an independent guest at Thanksgiving. 'You, Chan and the vein' — the casual inclusion of 'Chan' (not even Chandler) and then 'the vein' as the third party is excellent comedic construction. The word 'three' landing before the reveal is the structural setup that makes the punchline land. Very high quotability and probably the most rewatchable single-line joke in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I can't feel my ears!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait... I never could feel my ears. How do I know they're even there?

jokes.text: Joey gets his head stuck in the door chain. 'Stop, stop, I'm worried about damaging my head.' / 'It's a little late for that.'
jokes.setup: Joey tries to squeeze his head back through the door chain after the confrontation
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'It's a little late for that' — implying Joey's head has been damaged for years
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom zinger — the double meaning of 'damaging my head' played fast and clean. Monica's timing is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Tools? Oh sure, they're right next to my carpentry skills and my ability to be useful around the house. Which is to say, I have no idea where they are because I don't own any tools. I'm not a handyman. I'm a guy who once tried to hang a picture and ended up calling a professional.

jokes.text: Joey, as turkey grease is applied to his head to free it: "Oh, that smells good."
jokes.setup: Turkey grease is being smeared on Joey's stuck head to free him from the door chain
jokes.punchline: Joey's first instinct is not relief or embarrassment but sensory pleasure — the turkey smell is appealing despite the circumstance
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey. His head is physically stuck in a door chain, being greased, and all he can register is 'that smells good.' No other character on this show, or most shows, would have this response. Maximum character integration and economy — four words tell us everything about Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I borrowed them from Chandler, who borrowed them from Monica, who borrowed them from Ross. And I... left them at the park.

jokes.text: "Can you ever feel your ears?" / [pause] / "Interesting."
jokes.setup: Joey says he can't feel his ears while his head is stuck. Ross asks if he ever can.
jokes.punchline: Joey apparently has no immediate answer, implying he doesn't know whether he can normally feel his ears — and Ross's 'Interesting' treats this as a scientific data point
jokes.explanation: One of the more subtle gems in the episode. The implied pause where Joey can't answer, followed by Ross's 'Interesting' treating Joey's sensory self-ignorance as a research finding, is quietly very funny. Perfect economy — the joke lives in what isn't said.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more stuck?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Your head looks really big from this angle.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, and your butt is at a very unflattering height right now.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We should probably help him.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: In a minute.

jokes.text: "Chandler, where are your tools?" / "Oh, I left them on my bulldozer." / "I don't have tools."
jokes.setup: They need tools to unscrew the door chain and free Joey
jokes.punchline: Chandler's first response is sarcastic ('Oh, I left them on my bulldozer'), then his actual answer: he simply doesn't own tools
jokes.explanation: The bulldozer sarcasm is good; 'I don't have tools' as a flat confession is a solid beat. Chandler's domestic uselessness is consistent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Hello? Oh hi! No, I can't talk right now, I'm sorry. I have to go treat my varicose vein like it's the final authority on what I do with my time.

jokes.text: Tools chain: "I do, but Rachel borrowed them." / "I lent them to Ross." / "I gave them to Joey." / "I left them at the park."
jokes.setup: Everyone tries to identify whose tools can be used
jokes.punchline: The tools have passed through every character's hands like a hot potato and ended up lost at a park — an absurdist chain of domestic irresponsibility
jokes.explanation: The escalating chain is a classic bit — each reveal makes it worse, and Joey's 'I left them at the park' is the perfect final destination for a set of tools. Good rhythmic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Guys, come on! This isn't funny anymore!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, we're just getting started.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Please! I'm begging you!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What's the matter, Joe? Can't take a joke?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is not a joke! Let me out of here!

jokes.text: "I'm finding it really hard not to mess with him." / "I stuffed Brussels sprouts down his pants." / "Nice."
jokes.setup: Joey is stuck in the door chain. Monica has shown restraint.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe reveals she has been stuffing Brussels sprouts down Joey's pants while he was stuck — Monica's one-word approval: 'Nice'
jokes.explanation: Phoebe combining the Brussels sprouts callback with the Joey-stuck-in-door situation is inspired. The specificity of 'stuffed Brussels sprouts down his pants' is both funny and character-appropriate — Phoebe's chaotic energy, Monica's approving 'Nice,' Joey's helplessness. One of the standout moments of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What happened here?!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, there's food everywhere! It's like a crime scene committed by floating heads!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you know how long it takes to clean this? And you're just floating around here like some kind of disembodied—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? I don't even want to know. Just... floating heads. That's all I see now. Floating heads making messes in my apartment!

jokes.text: "Thanksgiving is over. The vein has spoken."
jokes.setup: Monica receives the adoption call in the middle of the door chaos
jokes.punchline: Chandler announces 'The vein has spoken' — the vein has been promoted from a physical feature to an oracle with authority over the holiday
jokes.explanation: The vein gag peaks here: 'The vein has spoken' is mock-biblical and treats the vein as a sovereign entity. Absurdist, quotable, economical. The running gag reaches its apex in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't even care about the mess anymore.

jokes.text: Thanksgiving is over. The vein has spoken.
jokes.setup: Monica announces that Thanksgiving is over and they should all leave
jokes.punchline: Chandler editorializes with 'The vein has spoken' — confirming the vein as an independent authority figure
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to the vein-as-third-party joke. 'The vein has spoken' has the cadence of an official decree — Chandler renders the vein's decision with the gravity of a Supreme Court pronouncement. It's the apex of the vein running gag and very quotable. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Last Thanksgiving, I was alone, crying into a bowl of sweet potatoes. This year, I have a baby!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So this is definitely better.

jokes.text: "My cranberries!" / "Man, I got food all over me."
jokes.setup: Everyone pushes the door simultaneously to free Joey; it flies open and food goes everywhere
jokes.punchline: Chandler's first thought is the cranberries — not anyone's safety, not the destruction — the cranberries
jokes.explanation: The final, definitive payoff of the cranberry running gag. Chandler crying 'My cranberries!' at the moment of maximum chaos is the emotional peak of his subplot — played entirely for comedy. Perfectly character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm so happy about the adoption!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's wonderful! We should totally put the baby in pageants!

jokes.text: "Look! Look! Look what the— Look what the floating heads did!"
jokes.setup: Food has been scattered everywhere by the door flying open
jokes.punchline: Monica, enraged, refers to the group as 'the floating heads' — her contempt has crystallized into adopting the absurdist label
jokes.explanation: Monica adopting 'floating heads' as a term of condemnation is a satisfying final callback. Her sputtering rage making her adopt Phoebe's absurdist label is a nice character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I totally get it. It's like when I was waiting for my action figure to come out. I kept calling the store, 'Is it here yet? Is it here yet?' Finally they said, 'Sir, we're going to have to ask you to stop calling.'

jokes.text: "This Thanksgiving kicks last Thanksgiving's ass!"
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler announce they're getting a baby
jokes.punchline: Joey's celebration takes the form of competitive Thanksgiving assessment — directly echoing Monica's 'In your face, last-year me' from the opening
jokes.explanation: Joey's crass but heartfelt line is a good mirror to Monica's self-competition at the top of the episode. The callback works emotionally and comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's like shopping for toys, you know? You go in, you see something you like, you take it home.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, Joey, adoption is exactly like shopping for toys. Except, you know, with less returning things and more permanent life-altering decisions.

jokes.text: "To Monica and Chandler and that knocked-up girl in Ohio."
jokes.setup: Everyone is toasting to the happy adoption news
jokes.punchline: Ross's toast reduces the birth mother to 'that knocked-up girl in Ohio' — an inadvertently crass summation from the group's most uptight member
jokes.explanation: The gap between the tender moment and Ross's clinical phrasing is good comedy. 'That knocked-up girl in Ohio' is unintentionally funny from Ross specifically because of his usual earnestness.

jokes.text: "Have you considered pageanting?"
jokes.setup: Everyone is emotional about Monica and Chandler getting a baby
jokes.punchline: Phoebe — immediately — pitches them on the baby pageant circuit, treating a newborn as a revenue opportunity
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode callback — Phoebe's first instinct on hearing about a future baby is to recruit them for pageants. 'Have you considered pageanting?' as a word (treating it as a verb) is economical and very Phoebe. High character integration.

jokes.text: "I know how you feel." / "Really?" / "Sure. I went through the exact same thing with Alicia May Emory. The waiting, the wondering. Then one day, I get that call from Toys 'R' Us. She was in stock." / "That is the exact same thing."
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are emotional about the adoption. Joey claims to relate.
jokes.punchline: Joey's parallel adoption experience is waiting for a Cabbage Patch Kid to be back in stock at Toys 'R' Us — and Chandler dryly confirms 'that is the exact same thing'
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best payoffs in the whole run of Friends Thanksgiving episodes. Joey drawing an earnest parallel between adoption and a Toys 'R' Us back-order call — with the SAME emotional weight, the same 'waiting and wondering' — is a perfect character joke. Alicia May Emory has been seeded twice, making the final mention land as a fully earned callback. Chandler's 'That is the exact same thing' as deadpan agreement is the perfect button. This is what a 9+ looks like in a Friends episode — it crystallizes Joey's lovable obliviousness at its absolute peak, is quotable, emotionally resonant, and structurally impeccable.

jokes.text: Sure. I went through the exact same thing with Alicia May Emory. The waiting, the wondering. Then one day, I get that call from Toys 'R' Us. She was in stock.
jokes.setup: Chandler says Ross can't know how it feels to wait for a child to come into your life
jokes.punchline: Ross equates the adoption experience to waiting for a Cabbage Patch doll to come back in stock at Toys R Us — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The setup is perfect — Chandler has just had the most significant moment of his life, and Ross says 'I know how you feel.' Then the full story: the waiting, the wondering, the call, 'she was in stock.' Each element is a perfect mirror of the adoption process, applied to a Cabbage Patch doll. The parallel structure ('the waiting, the wondering') mimics sincere emotional language and is completely deflated by 'Toys R Us' and 'she was in stock.' 'She was in stock' is the punchline within the punchline — it uses supply-chain retail language for what Ross experiences as a parental reunion. The structure earns a 9 because every element of the callback builds and pays off. Character integration is as high as it gets: only Ross, the goofy, earnest paleontologist with a named Cabbage Patch doll, could deliver this. The final line from Chandler ('That is the exact same thing') is the button.

tmdb_overview: Joey, Ross, Rachel and Phoebe convince Monica and Chandler to host a Thanksgiving dinner, however the four of them end up arriving an hour late as the boys decide to go to Rangers game, while the girls take Emma to a baby beauty pageant. This enrages Monica and she refuses to let the famished guests into her and Chandler's apartment which causes even bigger problems.
insight: Thanksgiving chaos delivers 87 jokes across 22 minutes—high volume, middling landing rate.
